title: Review --- Two Systems, Two New Words

lessons.title: Review — two systems, two new words
lessons.gloss: review — two systems, twelve cells, and only two of them new

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Nothing new. Two questions before the tables: where does an object pronoun go, and what single question chooses between the two sets?

utterances: me. direct — what: me. indirect — to whom: me.
you. direct — what: te. indirect — to whom: te.
him / her / usted. direct — what: lo, la. indirect — to whom: le.
us. direct — what: nos. indirect — to whom: nos.
you all (Spain). direct — what: os. indirect — to whom: os.
them / ustedes. direct — what: los, las. indirect — to whom: les.

segments.text: Twelve cells. Two of them are new since the last review, and you produced one of those yourself by adding an -s.

Do the arithmetic once and it will stay done. Fourteen chapters of object pronouns have asked you to learn, as shapes: te, lo, la, nos, os, le. Six words. Me you had from chapter four; los, las and les you derived. Six words, spread across fourteen chapters, with a review and a synthesis at each joint — that is what a gentle ramp costs and what it buys.
Read the third row again, because it is the only place the two columns disagree in shape rather than spelling:
direct: lo / la — two forms, gender marked. indirect: le — one form, gender not marked.

Spanish cares about the gender of a thing being acted on and does not care about the gender of a person being aimed at. There is no deep reason for it; Latin's dative simply had one form where its accusative had two, and Spanish inherited the asymmetry whole.
It is good news. The row that carries all the difficulty in one column carries none in the other.

segments.instruction: the direct six, then the indirect six, and hear how much is the same

segments.instruction: "lo tengo, le hablo, los tengo, les hablo"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "lo tengo, le hablo, los tengo, les hablo"]

segments.text: Until the shared four stop feeling like two separate lists.

segments.prompt: Give the six indirect object pronouns.
acceptedResponses: me, te, le, nos, os, les
me te le nos os les

feedback.correct: Four of them were already yours.
feedback.incorrect: me, te, le, nos, os, les.

segments.prompt: Which row is the only one where the two sets differ in shape, and how?
acceptedResponses: the him/her row: lo and la versus le

feedback.correct: Two forms in one column, one in the other.
feedback.incorrect: The him/her/usted row: direct has lo and la, indirect has only le.

segments.prompt: Across both tables, how many distinct word shapes are there in total?
acceptedResponses: me te lo la le nos os los las les

feedback.correct: Nine shapes covering twelve cells, because four do double duty.
feedback.incorrect: Nine: me, te, lo, la, le, nos, os, los, las, les — with four shared between the systems.

segments.text: How many pronouns are shared between the two sets? (Four.) Which row differs? (Him / her / usted — lo and la against le.) Next: both sets in one conversation, where you have to choose fast.
